The common dark pyroxene of basalt and gabbro; two cleavages at nearly 90°.

habits.l: Tabular to pyramidal triangular crystals; vivid blue

Hard beryllium oxide; forms heart-shaped twins and six-rayed trillings. Alexandrite changes colour in different light.

Bright orange lead chromate needles, best known from Tasmania; soft and heavy.
Copper oxide of oxidised copper deposits; dark red with a near-metallic shine.

habits.l: Short prismatic; vivid green from Cr3+

Pale grey to pale green, yellowish-brown

note: Magnesium orthopyroxene of peridotite and many meteorites.
Pistachio-green, striated prisms in altered igneous and metamorphic rocks.

Calcium–aluminium garnet of skarns and contact-metamorphosed limestone; tsavorite and hessonite are varieties.
Mohs 2 — you can scratch it with a fingernail. Evaporite mineral; selenite and desert rose are forms of it.

habits.l: Rounded dodecahedral to irregular; vivid violet-blue

habits.l: stubby prisms with a six-sided cross-section

Black octahedra that attract a magnet — the most magnetic natural mineral.

habits.l: Short prismatic with multiple dome forms

High-temperature potassium feldspar of volcanic rocks such as rhyolite and trachyte.
Square prisms in marbles and skarns; often fluoresces yellow.

Emerald-green chromium garnet; usually tiny crystals coating chromite.

Thin orange-yellow square plates of lead molybdate from oxidised lead deposits.
